御香宮.note: The Gokō-no-miya shrine at Fushimi; its wooded precinct became the Satsuma army's forward post in 1868, directly north of the Magistracy.

林権助.note: Hayashi Gonsuke (Yasusada), the 63-year-old Aizu commissioner of artillery who commanded the Aizu contingent at Fushimi; killed in the fighting there.

王政復古.note: The Ōsei Fukko coup of Keiō 3/12/9 (3 January 1868): the shogunate and regency abolished, direct Imperial rule declared.

ch39.anchor: the eighteenth of the eleventh month, in the third year of Keiō
ch39.note: The Aburanokōji Incident. The lunar date Keiō 3/11/18 converts to 13 December 1867. Kondō lured Itō to his residence, plied him with drink, and had him speared and cut down on his way home near the Aburanokōji; the corps then left the body as bait and ambushed the Goryō-eji who came to recover it, killing Tōdō Heisuke, Hattori Takeo, and Mōnai (Kenmotsu). The novel makes the swordsman who finished Itō one Mutō Katsuzō; other accounts name Ōishi Kuwajirō among the assassins. The sequence of events is well attested.

Sei-i Taishōgun, 'Great General who Subdues the Barbarians,' the full title of which 'shogun' is the everyday abbreviation. First given to commanders sent against the Emishi of the north, it became from the twelfth century the title of the hereditary military ruler of Japan.

Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), founder of the Kamakura shogunate and the first warrior to rule Japan as Sei-i Taishōgun. Kondō's point is that a warrior house had held real power for the near seven centuries since.

Yoshitsune (1159–1189), Yoritomo's younger half-brother and the most dazzling commander of the Genpei War, hunted to his death by the very brother he had won the war for. He is the proverbial beautiful, doomed, melancholy hero — hence Toshizō's jibe about a chief who broods 'with a pale face like some Yoshitsune.'
Mount Tai (Taizan) in Shandong, foremost of China's five sacred peaks and a stock image for massive, unshakable steadiness.

The Western folding umbrella (kōmori-gasa, 'bat umbrella'), so named for its black ribs and cloth. A novelty of the treaty-port years; that hatamoto and then townsmen were carrying it marks how fast Edo was Westernizing by 1867.

ch39.anchor: There were no fireworks at Ryōgoku this year
ch39.note: The summer fireworks over the Sumida River at Ryōgoku Bridge had been an Edo institution since the 1730s. Their cancellation registers the unsettled, money-short mood of the capital in the last year of the shogunate.

Jōfu: retainers of a domain posted permanently to Edo rather than rotating home under the alternate-attendance system. Their children were Edo-born and Edo-bred, which is why Nagakura's homesickness for the city runs deeper than the others'.

ch39.anchor: he changed his name to Kashitarō to mark it
ch39.note: Itō took the name Kashitarō (甲子太郎) to commemorate the sexagenary year kinoe-ne (1864) in which he joined the Shinsengumi; on defecting to Satsuma he changed it again, to Settsu. The serial renaming, the narrator notes, was peculiarly his own habit.
The Noh play Chikubushima, named for the island shrine of the goddess Benzaiten in Lake Biwa. That Itō is cut off mid-chant lends the killing its theatrical hush.

ch40.anchor: unmoving as a mountain, unhurried as a forest
ch40.note: An echo of Sun Tzu — 'swift as the wind, quiet as the forest, fierce as fire, immovable as the mountain' — the maxim Takeda Shingen bore on his war-banner (fū-rin-ka-zan). It is Toshizō's ideal for the corps, and he quotes another strain of it aloud a few lines on.

Toshizō names the standard reading of a half-schooled samurai: the Analects of Confucius and the Mencius; the Jūhasshiryaku, a Yuan-dynasty digest of Chinese history long used as a Japanese primer; and the Nihon Gaishi, Rai San'yō's popular history of the warrior houses.
The two Chinese classics of war: the Sunzi (Sun Tzu's Art of War) and the Wuzi, ascribed to the general Wu Qi. Toshizō prefers these books of pure tactics to the moralizing histories.

ch40.anchor: the way a bystander reads a game of go
ch40.note: From the proverb okame-hachimoku: the onlooker at a game of go sees eight moves further than the players absorbed in it. Toshizō means that book-learning only sets a man second-guessing his own resolve.

ch40.anchor: on the second day of the fifth month of the thirty-first year of Meiji
ch40.note: That is, 2 May 1898. Yoshinobu (1837–1913) lived out his thirty-year retirement in near-total seclusion and was only then received again by the Emperor Meiji — the measure, for Shiba, of the completeness of his self-effacement.

ch41.anchor: boasted the authority of the Tokugawa
ch41.note: The Fushimi Magistracy (bugyōsho), the shogunate's administrative and judicial seat for the Fushimi post-town and its river port south of Kyoto. Its walled compound made a natural forward strongpoint; the next chapter finds the site built over as a housing estate.

The nine gates (kumon) of the outer enclosure of the Kyoto palace. To be commanded to guard them was to be received back as a trusted Imperial force — a total reversal of Chōshū's disgrace after the Hamaguri Gate affair of 1864, and a sign of how far Satsuma had turned the court.

The Minié rifle, a muzzle-loader firing the expanding conical Minié ball; its rifled barrel gave range and accuracy far beyond the old smoothbore musket. Its spread is the material fact behind Chōshū's transformation in four years.
The 'four-kin' (yonkin) gun, a light rifled field piece throwing roughly a four-pound shell — the modern French-derived artillery of the new-model armies, outranging the shogunal side's smoothbores.
The Geweer (Japanese geberu), a Dutch smoothbore percussion musket without even a rear sight: obsolete beside the rifled Minié, and typical of the shogunal side's mixed, dated equipment.

A married woman of the townsman and samurai classes shaved her eyebrows (and blackened her teeth); unshaved brows mark this woman as keeping the presentation of a maiden or an independent widow rather than a matron. Toshizō is describing Oyuki, a samurai widow.

ch42.anchor: turned again at the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch42.note: The Battle of Toba-Fushimi (Keiō 4/1/3–6, i.e. 27–30 January 1868), the opening clash of the Boshin War, fought on the roads into Kyoto from the south. Though heavily outnumbered, the Satsuma-Chōshū forces broke the shogunal army; when the Imperial brocade banner was raised, the Tokugawa side became 'rebels,' and the campaign was decided. Well attested.
The battle of Sekigahara (1600), at which Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory made him master of Japan and founded the order that Toba-Fushimi would bring down.

Matsumoto Ryōjun (1832–1907), later Matsumoto Jun: shogunal physician, pupil of the Dutch doctor Pompe, founder of Japan's first Western hospital at Nagasaki, and after the Restoration the army's first surgeon-general and a baron. Shiba's aside that he opened Japan's first sea-bathing beach is right in substance but wrong in place — the beach was at Ōiso (1885), not Zushi, as the author's own hedge, 'Zushi, I believe,' half-concedes.
J. L. C. Pompe van Meerdervoort (1829–1908), the Dutch naval surgeon who from 1857 gave Japan its first systematic instruction in Western medicine, at Nagasaki.
Hōgen ('Eye of the Law'), in origin a Buddhist clerical rank, was granted by the court as an honorary title to eminent physicians, painters, and other men of skill.

ch42.anchor: the Winter and Summer Sieges of Osaka
ch42.note: The two campaigns of 1614–15 in which Ieyasu manufactured pretexts to destroy the Toyotomi house — reduced by then to a single great domain at Osaka — that his own overlord's heir, Hideyori, still headed. Toshizō sees the same maneuver being worked on the Tokugawa now, and in the same castle.

Mitogaku, the historiography built around the Dai Nihonshi compiled by the Mito Tokugawa, which judged the past by loyalty to the throne and branded the disloyal 'enemies of the Court.' Yoshinobu, a Mito son, could not bear to wear that name — the flaw, Shiba argues, that unmanned him.

The tōsatsu-hyō, the manifesto under which the shogunal army marched on Kyoto, cast as a petition to the throne against the Satsuma 'traitors.' By 'rising to the challenge' with it, the Tokugawa side gave Satsuma exactly the war it wanted.

ch43.anchor: which one might call a second Warring-States age in the nation
ch43.note: 'Boshin' is the sexagenary name of the year 1868 (Keiō 4 / Meiji 1), and the war that opens here is named from it. Shiba's 'second Warring-States age' looks back to the century of sixteenth-century civil war that Ieyasu had ended.
The shirasu, the white-graveled forecourt of a magistracy, where the accused knelt and sentence was pronounced — a fitting seat for the corps that had policed Kyoto by the sword.

The corps' own standard bore the single character makoto ('sincerity'). Over it they now flew the Rising-Sun ensign as the flag of the whole shogunal army, in the conviction that theirs was Japan's lawful government. The claim would collapse within days: once the Imperial brocade banner (nishiki no mihata) was carried over the Satsuma-Chōshū side, the Tokugawa army became, in law, a rebel host.

ch43.anchor: commander of the Fourth Army in the Russo-Japanese War
ch43.note: Nozu Michitsura (1841–1908) rose to field marshal and commanded the Fourth Army against Russia in 1904–05; his elder brother Shizuo, the outpost captain here, also became a general. Shiba's habit of flashing forward to these junior officers' later eminence measures how many of Meiji's commanders were blooded at Toba-Fushimi.

Ōyama Iwao (1842–1916), the young Satsuma gunner on Ryūunji-yama, became army minister, field marshal, and commander-in-chief of the Manchurian armies against Russia — one of the towering figures of the Meiji state.

The Asobi (elsewhere the ju) were the neighborhood bands into which the sons of upper Aizu samurai were grouped from about age six; each afternoon's meeting opened with the recited code Shiba gives here, which in its full form ended with the famous line, 'What must not be done, must not be done.' It bred the ferocious discipline that would make Aizu's stand — and its tragedy — in this war.
The Naganuma-ryū of military science (gungaku), the tradition of tactics and drill in which the Aizu domain trained its troops.

ch43.anchor: the Great Elder of the shogunal council
ch43.note: The tairō ('Great Elder'), the highest office of the shogunate, filled only in a crisis and by custom from a few premier hereditary houses — the Ii of Hikone chief among them, whose Ii Naosuke had held it at the time of the Perry treaties. Their going over to Satsuma is thus a defection of the Tokugawa vanguard itself.

ch43.anchor: became the first shot of the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch43.note: The shell from Nozu's Satsuma battery, fired about 5 p.m. on Keiō 4/1/3 (27 January 1868), was indeed the first shot of Toba-Fushimi and so of the Boshin War. Contemporary accounts agree the Satsuma side fired first, a bursting shell throwing the shogunal column into confusion. Well attested.
